What it solves, how it works, and how to integrate it into a CKB application
Imagine building an application on Nervos CKB where a user deposits an asset today but should not be able to spend it until a future date. The same requirement might arise in token vesting, a treasury release, or a payment-channel dispute period. The Cell exists, and someone may already be authorized to spend it. The missing piece is time: the transaction should not be valid yet.
CKB addresses this need through `since`, a small transaction-input field with an important purpose: expressing when an input is eligible to be committed. Once you understand that role, since becomes useful well beyond a simple timelock.
What is 'Since
`since` is an optional, consensus-enforced maturity condition on each CKB transaction input. When a transaction consumes an existing Cell, the network checks the input’s `since` value. If it specifies a condition that has not matured, the transaction cannot be committed—even when its other requirements are satisfied. A value of zero disables the `since` precondition.
It is useful to think of `since` as a “not before” rule, not as an instruction to execute a transaction on a schedule. Once the condition matures, someone must still construct, authorize, and submit the spending transaction.
A key distinction: `since` belongs to the spending transaction input, not to the existing Cell or the newly created output. Each input can carry its own condition.
What is Solves and Why CKB needs it.
The Cell Model changes state by consuming existing Cells and creating new ones. Lock scripts determine whether a spending transaction meets the rules protecting those Cells. Authorization and maturity, however, answer different questions: who is allowed to spend, and when is the spending transaction allowed to be committed?
Consider a vesting allocation owned by an employee, a treasury held until a governance deadline, or a payment-channel refund path that should become available only after a challenge period. Knowing the authorized party is not enough; the transaction also needs a maturity rule.
Rather than leaving every protocol to devise its own view of time, CKB defines `since` at the consensus layer. Because the field is per input, one transaction can combine Cells with different maturity requirements. All of those inputs must be mature for the transaction to be committed.
The features of Since.
1. Three measurement of maturity.
RFC 0017 provides three metrics. Block number expresses a particular height or number of blocks; epoch number expresses CKB’s epoch structure, including fractional positions; and timestamp expresses time in milliseconds using the blockchain’s consensus-defined timestamp rule. The metric should match the application’s intended behavior.
Block number — suitable for rules defined by chain progression, such as a 100-block waiting period.
Epoch number with fraction — suitable for rules naturally expressed in CKB epochs.
Timestamp — suitable for user-facing deadlines and durations expressed in real-world time.
2. Absolute and relative conditions
Absolute `since` names a fixed maturity point. “Not before block 1,000,000” is absolute, regardless of when the Cell was created. Relative `since` defines a delay measured from the referenced Cell’s commitment: “wait 100 blocks after this Cell was committed.”
These meanings must not be confused. At chain height 25,000, absolute block 100 has already matured; relative block delay 100 is a different condition. Both modes are available for block, epoch, and timestamp metrics.
3. `since` is not a timer
A maturity condition does not count down inside the Cell, wake up a contract, or automatically broadcast a transaction. It is evaluated when a spending transaction is processed. The application—or another authorized actor—must still submit a valid transaction after maturity.
4. `since` is an encoded `u64`
The field is a 64-bit unsigned integer, but not all 64 bits represent time. Bit 63 selects relative versus absolute mode; bits 62–61 select the metric (block, epoch, or timestamp); bits 60–56 are reserved and must be zero; and the lower 56 bits hold the encoded value. The metric pattern `11` is invalid.
5. Timestamp maturity uses CKB consensus time
A device clock showing that a deadline has passed does not prove the transaction is mature. For timestamp-based `since`, CKB checks a consensus-derived median of the preceding 37 block timestamps. Accordingly, an application may show the user’s local time for convenience, but should use the chain’s maturity rule to determine whether spending is eligible.
How to integrate `since` into a CKB project
The implementation starts with an application rule, not a bit mask. The same sequence applies whether the client is written in Rust, TypeScript, another language, or built with a framework.
1. Define the rule. State the requirement precisely: a fixed date, a target block, or a duration after commitment.
2. Choose the mode and metric. Select absolute or relative, then block number, epoch, or timestamp.
3. Encode the value. Use RFC 0017’s 64-bit format. Validate the permitted range, flag combination, and reserved bits.
4. Commit the required spending policy to the Cell. If the delay must be mandatory, the lock must authenticate and enforce the intended policy, for example using lock arguments or Cell data.
5. Create and commit the protected Cell. Construct the creation transaction and confirm commitment. Relative conditions rely on the referenced Cell’s on-chain commitment point.
6. Construct the spending transaction. Reference the Cell’s OutPoint, set the encoded `since` on that input, construct outputs, and supply dependencies and witnesses.
7. Enforce the spending rules. The lock script verifies its authorization and policy requirements, including the prescribed mode, metric, and value. Where a script group includes multiple applicable inputs, validate each one.
8. Let consensus evaluate maturity. CKB checks whether each input’s `since` precondition is mature. The transaction can be committed only when all applicable consensus and script rules pass.
9. Test failure paths. Verify premature spending, wrong mode or metric, invalid bits, policy bypass with `since = 0`, unauthorized spending, and multiple-input behavior.
Trade-offs and design choices
Absolute versus relative — an absolute deadline is known in advance, but late Cell commitment shortens the effective holding period. Relative maturity preserves a commitment-based delay, while its exact target depends on when the Cell is committed.
Blocks versus wall-clock time — a block count is easy to use for protocol delays, but variable block production prevents it from guaranteeing an exact number of minutes.
Epoch versus timestamp — epochs align with CKB’s native progress model but are harder to present to ordinary users; timestamps communicate dates clearly but rely on consensus time, not a local device clock.
Consensus enforcement versus automation — consensus checks when spending is eligible, but it does not schedule or execute the transaction for the application.
Flexible encoding versus correctness — the compact format supports several time models, but developers must decode the flags and enforce the intended policy rather than compare raw `u64` values.
Per-input conditions versus transaction-wide maturity — independent inputs can express independent deadlines, but one immature input prevents commitment of the entire transaction.
Conclusion
`since` gives a CKB transaction input a consensus-level “not before” rule. Developers choose the appropriate time model, encode it correctly, and—when the application requires a mandatory lock—make the Cell’s script enforce that policy. CKB consensus determines whether the spending input has matured.
The practical takeaway is to separate three concerns: who may spend, what maturity policy the application requires, and whether the blockchain has reached that condition. Keeping those responsibilities distinct makes time-based CKB applications easier to reason about and safer to implement.

Q3 2026 Report
Executive summary
Q3 brought further growth across Nervos Community Catalyst’s developer programmes and community activity. CKBuilders grew to close to 100 active builders and alumni, while Build on CKB campaigns continued to challenge developers to advance their CKB skills. The project tracker expanded from 45 projects at the end of Q2 to 59 by the beginning of October, and 18 projects were submitted for review during the quarter. The Gone in 60ms Fiber Network Infrastructure Hackathon brought together roughly 100 participants and received 66 submissions.
Alongside supporting individual developers and projects, NCC saw interest from teams outside the CKB ecosystem and strengthened in-person connections through CKB Off-Chain with events in Nairobi, Vietnam, and elsewhere. CKBoost reached around 150 users, generating testing data, bug reports and feedback to inform its next stage.
Community Keeps Building
CKBuilders
CKBuilders continued to grow in Q3, with over 25 new builders joining, predominantly from Vietnam and Indonesia. We have prioritised expanding to new regions that have thriving blockchain communities in order to continue building global awareness of CKB. The number of active CKBuilders and alumni now stands at close to 100.
Alumni are developers who have completed the programme and remain part of the CKBuilders peer learning group. Those who continue to build retain access to our shared AI resources, while some alumni have progressed to projects supported by the Spark Programme or the Community Fund DAO.
The programme design allows us to continue to grow efficiently, bringing more developers into the community without creating a dependency or increasing overheads. The key is to continue to spread CKB to new developers and enrich our community with fresh perspectives and opportunities.
Build on CKB
Build on CKB is the Telegram group for all new community developers, where they can get started with building on CKB through campaigns based on introductory tutorials. During Q3, numerous campaigns were completed, as listed on CKBoost:
Build on CKB Campaign 03: Build a Simple Lock tutorial. 25 participants
Build on CKB Campaign 04: Create a DOB tutorial. 20 participants
Build on CKB Campaign 05: Create a Fungible Token. 20 participants
Build on CKB Campaign 06: Fiber startup and test payment. 24 participants.
For the most recent campaign, I must thank the DevRel team for collaborating to deliver it, and to @yuqi for its design and execution.
Future activities will center around new campaigns focused on Fiber. We will also periodically revisit previous campaigns so newer group entrants can still participate at a level comfortable for them.
Developer articles
As their understanding of CKB deepens, CKBuilders have added further articles to the Knowledge Base, exploring interesting questions or reflecting on the developer experience:
On CKB, You Drive: A Guide for Polkadot Developers by @Mulandi_Cecilia
Reflections of a CKBuilder: Bitcoin Doesn’t Know It Has Smart Contracts by @WuodOdhis
Following on from Where Is the ABI? Also, Why Is My Cell Dead? , @xiaomao posted follow up articles:
The Proof Is Valid. The Transition Might Not Be
When the Proof Finally Met the Cell
Project tracker
The CKBuilder project tracker grew from 45 projects at the end of Q2 to 59 by the beginning of October. The new entries covered a wide range of work, including developer tools, prediction markets, games, credentials, time-locked vaults and payment infrastructure.
Examples include LS-IDL, a tool for describing lock script interfaces; CKB Script Port, for transferring synced script data between light-client installations; noir-ckb, exploring proof-bound CKB transactions; and LucentDEx, an order-book exchange prototype. The tracker also added projects such as a Fiber-based survival game, a football prediction market and Klavernoq, a work marketplace built on PactAgent infrastructure.
Additionally, 18 projects were submitted for review through the CKBuilder review request page in Q3. The review process has proved to be a valuable source of feedback to developers as they refine their ideas and designs, so I must thank everyone who has participated in helping to conduct reviews.
Whilst many projects remain prototypes or works in progress, publishing them in one place makes the breadth of experimentation visible and gives community members a starting point for following or testing projects, or inspiration for their own ideas. Importantly, as I mention in my conclusion, renewed emphasis must be given towards creating projects which have sound business, as well as technical, rationale.
Progression to Community Fund DAO
In Q3, Fiber Desktop by @ebubedev and FiberLatch by @Ticoworld completed their proposed development, and continue to be maintained.
Vellum, the DID and reputation protocol built on did:ckb by @truthixify, passed the governance process on its second attempt and its work is ongoing.
Other proposals include:
Kaze Uni tour continuation, by @Dorex45, stage 1 voting passed
CrowdCell all-or-nothing crowdfunding platform, by @Ayoub_Lesfer, stage 1 voting passed
Rivet - decentralized GitHub backup, timestamping and restore on CKB, by @Jedi_dtechmaker, stage 2 voting passed
Teams come to CKB
Alongside the growth of individual builders, we have seen increased interest from external teams willing to explore building on CKB.
Lucent Labs, a team from Cardano and Midnight, is developing an open-source order-book DEX proof of concept.
Kaze, a team working with Bitcoin and Lightning, is exploring the integration of CKB and Fiber into its geolocation rewards app.
TexLabs, also from Cardano and Midnight, is exploring the intersection of AI and payment channels, as well as CKB payments over Lightning.
Gone in 60ms: Building Fiber Infrastructure
The Gone in 60ms Fiber Network Infrastructure Hackathon ran through July. It attracted roughly 100 participants and received 66 submissions across three categories: wallet and payment UX; node, routing, cross-chain and diagnostics infrastructure; and merchant, liquidity, LSP and multi-asset infrastructure. Clasp was named the overall winner, with Fiber Forge and FiberNuts taking first place in their respective categories
The submissions included practical infrastructure for controlling app access to Fiber nodes, setting up local Fiber development networks, and enabling Cashu-based assets to settle over Fiber. The results showed a substantial volume of work focused on reusable tools and infrastructure.
Creating long-lasting endeavours
One objective of hackathons is to produce new projects and ideas that leave a lasting contribution to the ecosystem. Whilst there are numerous projects with some level of work ongoing, two in particular stand out at this stage:
Klaveroq is being developed on PactAgent infrastructure as a jobs marketplace supported by agent-mediated workflow and escrow on CKB. PactAgent won the previous Claw & Order AI Agent Hackathon, and Klaveroq is an example of a project building a product on top of that work.
FiberNuts, the first-place project in the hackathon’s third category, is continuing to work towards a viable implementation, having created a FiberNuts Community Market. This demo shows how Cashu and Fiber could support small event payments. Attendees add RUSD ecash through Fiber, then use it to pay vendors; vendors can later cash out through Fiber.
Adapting to growth
A key challenge for NCC will be adapting its operating capacity to the scale of these programmes. As participation grows, we will need to continue improving communication, organisation, developer mentorship, the developer experience and our tracking of community activity.
CKB Off-Chain
Nairobi
Following the first Africa-based CKB Off-Chain meetup in Lagos, we continued building connections in East Africa with the Nairobi meetup on 18 July, held in collaboration with Web3Clubs. Around 45 people attended, including local CKBuilders, developers already familiar with CKB and people encountering the ecosystem for the first time. CKBuilders and other contributors presented their work, while discussion highlighted interest in stablecoins, local payment systems and the potential for Fiber in the Kenyan market. The event helped strengthen existing relationships and introduced CKB to developers in Nairobi.
Hanoi
Just after the close of Q3, CKB Off-Chain Hanoi took place on 8 October at Nguyen Trai University, in collaboration with BPS Club and Tex Labs. The event brought together Vietnamese CKBuilders, software developers, students and faculty members. Local builders presented projects and shared their experience, alongside sessions on CKB fundamentals, post-quantum cryptography, hardware wallets and Fiber. It was the first CKB Off-Chain event in Vietnam centred on CKBuilders and their experiences, and represents an initial step towards further developer engagement and education in the region.
Community-led events
A notable development is that CKB community developers are beginning to organise events of their own. Recent examples include:
Kaze Uni tour, Mombasa: Held at the Technical University of Mombasa in August, the event introduced students to Bitcoin, CKB and self-custody. Around 95% of attendees were new to Bitcoin, and 58 created CKB wallets and tried Kaze’s location-based rewards app. Organised by the Kaze team.
CKB Off-Chain Aba: Held on 3 October with Abia Web3 Network, the meetup featured presentations on RIVET, CKB IDL and Freight on Nervos, and connected local developers to CKB, with good turnout despite heavy rain. Organised by @Jedi_dtechmaker
CKB community meetup, Kisumu: Another community-organised meetup took place in Kisumu on October 16, with a write-up still to come. Organised by @Fidelcoder
We will continue to support community developer events in Nigeria, Kenya and Vietnam, while exploring new locations where groups of CKBuilders are developing.
CKBoost
With the ongoing Build on CKB campaigns and Fiber hackathon mentioned above, CKBoost has continued to build a developer user base, now numbering at around 150. The priority this quarter was to build CKBoost’s user base, validating the its usefulness as a campaign platform. This has facilitated valuable testing data, bug reports and feedback that helps inform the next stage of CKBoost development. The focus for CKBoost moving forward will be to improve the UX, remove points of friction, and refine the design to make it viable for mainnet. As ever, thanks to @Alive24 for his continued work on this.
Looking forward
NCC’s next phase will focus on supporting this growth with stronger communication, organisation, developer mentorship, developer experience and tracking of community activity. This will allow community activities to be more visible internally and externally. Planning will begin for the next Fiber hackathon, focusing on products and market-facing applications. Linked to this is the challenge of helping builders progress from demo creation and community grants towards market strategy and business viability. This will be a key concern to address in future.
We will support community developer events in Nigeria, Kenya and Vietnam, while exploring new locations where CKBuilder groups are developing, in particular South East Asia. We will also support builders as their projects develop and, where appropriate, progress through the Community Fund DAO and other ecosystem pathways.

  • Kaze Uni tour, Mombasa: Held at the Technical University of Mombasa in August, the event introduced students to Bitcoin, CKB and self-custody. Around 95% of attendees were new to Bitcoin, and 58 created CKB wallets and tried Kaze’s location-based rewards app. Organised by the Kaze team.
  • CKB Off-Chain Aba: Held on 3 October with Abia Web3 Network, the meetup featured presentations on RIVET, CKB IDL and Freight on Nervos, and connected local developers to CKB, with good turnout despite heavy rain. Organised by @Jedi_dtechmaker
  • CKB community meetup, Kisumu: Another community-organised meetup took place in Kisumu on October 16, with a write-up still to come. Organised by @Fidelcoder

We will continue to support community developer events in Nigeria, Kenya and Vietnam, while exploring new locations where groups of CKBuilders are developing.

CKBoost

With the ongoing Build on CKB campaigns and Fiber hackathon mentioned above, CKBoost has continued to build a developer user base, now numbering at around 150. The priority this quarter was to build CKBoost’s user base, validating the its usefulness as a campaign platform. This has facilitated valuable testing data, bug reports and feedback that helps inform the next stage of CKBoost development. The focus for CKBoost moving forward will be to improve the UX, remove points of friction, and refine the design to make it viable for mainnet. As ever, thanks to @Alive24 for his continued work on this.

Looking forward

NCC’s next phase will focus on supporting this growth with stronger communication, organisation, developer mentorship, developer experience and tracking of community activity. This will allow community activities to be more visible internally and externally. Planning will begin for the next Fiber hackathon, focusing on products and market-facing applications. Linked to this is the challenge of helping builders progress from demo creation and community grants towards market strategy and business viability. This will be a key concern to address in future.

We will support community developer events in Nigeria, Kenya and Vietnam, while exploring new locations where CKBuilder groups are developing, in particular South East Asia. We will also support builders as their projects develop and, where appropriate, progress through the Community Fund DAO and other ecosystem pathways.

recent_posts.content_html:
Hi everyone,

Back in April I posted a revamp of the CKB wallet connection UI as a compound React component on top of CCC. The feedback from CKB builders was consistent: this should be installable as a package, not something you copy out of a demo.

That package is now live as ckb-connect-wallet-kit. You wrap your own ccc.Provider, compose the button / icon / balance / address yourself, and optionally show the connected lock’s did:ckb avatar, display name, and identifier. The kit never mounts CCC. Current version is 0.2.1.

Links

  • npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/ckb-connect-wallet-kit

  • Homepage / demo: https://ckb-connect-wallet-kit.vercel.app/

  • GitHub repo: GitHub - Victor-Okenwa/revamp-ckb-connect-wallet: A compound component of the CKB connect wallet to improve developer experience. · GitHub

  • My GitHub: Victor-Okenwa (Okenwa victor) · GitHub

  • Earlier thread: Revamping and Refactoring the CKB Wallet Connection Experience: A Modular Compound Component for React Developers

What it is

ckb-connect-wallet-kit is a compound React UI for [@ckb-ccc/connector-react](``https://www.npmjs.com/package/@ckb-ccc/connector-react``). Shared state (wallet, address, balance, open()) lives in React context, so there is no prop drilling. A value on a single piece overrides the matching provider default.

What you get:

  • Compose the exact connected-wallet UI you want

  • One fetch for address and balance (Promise.all)

  • Loading pulses on the button and the connected pill

  • Provider-level defaults, overridable per instance

  • Balance control: decimalPlaces (0–20) truncates, does not round; optional CKB suffix

  • Address control: keep frontChars and endChars, the middle becomes ...

  • ConnectWalletButton hides after connect; the info pieces render only then

  • Optional did:ckb profile for the connected lock

  • TypeScript types for defaults, DecimalPlaces, and DidProfile

Creating or editing a DID is a signed CKB transaction and is outside this kit. The DID pieces only read live did:ckb cells owned by the connected lock.

What it requires

Peer dependencies:

  • react and react-dom (^18.3.1)

  • @ckb-ccc/connector-react (^1.0.0)

You must mount your own ccc.Provider. ConnectWallet and ConnectWalletKitProvider both call ccc.useCcc(), so they throw if CCC is missing.

The components ship Tailwind class names, not a prebuilt stylesheet. Tailwind v4 does not scan node_modules unless you point it at the package.

Install

npm install ckb-connect-wallet-kit @ckb-ccc/connector-react react react-dom

Same packages with pnpm / yarn / bun:

pnpm add ckb-connect-wallet-kit @ckb-ccc/connector-react react react-dom
yarn add ckb-connect-wallet-kit @ckb-ccc/connector-react react react-dom
bun add ckb-connect-wallet-kit @ckb-ccc/connector-react react react-dom

Then in your CSS:

@import "tailwindcss";
@source "../node_modules/ckb-connect-wallet-kit/dist";

Adjust the @source path if your CSS file sits somewhere else relative to node_modules.

How to use it

The pieces have built-in styles. Leave off className, formatting props, and defaults to use them as-is.

1. CCC provider, no styling

Your ccc.Provider plus the kit pieces. No ConnectWalletKitProvider, no defaults, no className.

import { ccc } from "@ckb-ccc/connector-react";
import {
  ConnectWallet,
  ConnectWalletButton,
  ConnectWalletInfoContainer,
  ConnectWalletInfoImage,
  ConnectWalletInfoBalance,
  ConnectWalletInfoAddress,
} from "ckb-connect-wallet-kit";

export function App() {
  return (
    <ccc.Provider
      defaultClient={new ccc.ClientPublicTestnet()}
      clientOptions={[
        { name: "CKB Testnet", client: new ccc.ClientPublicTestnet() },
        { name: "CKB Mainnet", client: new ccc.ClientPublicMainnet() },
      ]}
    >
      <ConnectWallet>
        <ConnectWalletButton />
        <ConnectWalletInfoContainer>
          <ConnectWalletInfoImage />
          <ConnectWalletInfoBalance />
          <ConnectWalletInfoAddress />
        </ConnectWalletInfoContainer>
      </ConnectWallet>
    </ccc.Provider>
  );
}

The button uses the built-in pill. After connect it hides, and the container shows the icon, the full formatted balance with CKB, and an address truncated to 10 + 6 characters.

2. Kit provider, no defaults

Same CCC tree. ConnectWalletKitProvider only opens the defaults context. Omit defaults so every composition uses the built-in look. Style or format a single piece with props when you need to.

import { ccc } from "@ckb-ccc/connector-react";
import {
  ConnectWalletKitProvider,
  ConnectWallet,
  ConnectWalletButton,
  ConnectWalletInfoContainer,
  ConnectWalletInfoImage,
  ConnectWalletInfoBalance,
  ConnectWalletInfoAddress,
} from "ckb-connect-wallet-kit";

export function App() {
  return (
    <ccc.Provider
      defaultClient={new ccc.ClientPublicTestnet()}
      clientOptions={[
        { name: "CKB Testnet", client: new ccc.ClientPublicTestnet() },
        { name: "CKB Mainnet", client: new ccc.ClientPublicMainnet() },
      ]}
    >
      <ConnectWalletKitProvider>
        <ConnectWallet>
          <ConnectWalletButton>Connect</ConnectWalletButton>
          <ConnectWalletInfoContainer>
            <ConnectWalletInfoImage />
            <ConnectWalletInfoBalance decimalPlaces={4} withCurrency />
            <ConnectWalletInfoAddress frontChars={6} endChars={4} />
          </ConnectWalletInfoContainer>
        </ConnectWallet>
      </ConnectWalletKitProvider>
    </ccc.Provider>
  );
}

3. Kit provider, with defaults

Set look and formatting once. A prop on one piece still wins over the matching default.

import { ccc } from "@ckb-ccc/connector-react";
import {
  ConnectWalletKitProvider,
  ConnectWallet,
  ConnectWalletButton,
  ConnectWalletInfoContainer,
  ConnectWalletInfoImage,
  ConnectWalletInfoBalance,
  ConnectWalletInfoAddress,
} from "ckb-connect-wallet-kit";

export function App() {
  return (
    <ccc.Provider
      defaultClient={new ccc.ClientPublicTestnet()}
      clientOptions={[
        { name: "CKB Testnet", client: new ccc.ClientPublicTestnet() },
        { name: "CKB Mainnet", client: new ccc.ClientPublicMainnet() },
      ]}
    >
      <ConnectWalletKitProvider
        defaults={{
          buttonClassName: "rounded-md bg-blue-600 text-white dark:bg-blue-600 dark:text-white",
          infoContainerClassName: "rounded-md bg-blue-600 text-white dark:bg-blue-600 dark:text-white",
          decimalPlaces: 4,
          withCurrency: true,
          frontChars: 6,
          endChars: 4,
          buttonLabel: "Connect Wallet",
        }}
      >
        <ConnectWallet>
          <ConnectWalletButton />
          <ConnectWalletInfoContainer className="flex items-center gap-2">
            <ConnectWalletInfoImage />
            <div className="flex flex-col items-start">
              <ConnectWalletInfoBalance />
              <ConnectWalletInfoAddress />
            </div>
          </ConnectWalletInfoContainer>
        </ConnectWallet>
      </ConnectWalletKitProvider>
    </ccc.Provider>
  );
}

className is merged after the provider class, so conflicting Tailwind utilities on that instance win.

LayoutProvider is the previous name of ConnectWalletKitProvider. Same props. It does not mount CCC.

How class names and defaults resolve

For appearance classes:

  1. Built-in styles (used when that default is omitted)

  2. defaults.*ClassName from ConnectWalletKitProvider

  3. className on the component (merged last)

For values (decimalPlaces, withCurrency, frontChars, endChars, didFrontChars, didEndChars, button label):

  1. Built-in fallback

  2. defaults.* from the provider

  3. The prop on the component (wins)

ClassValue is the clsx input type: a string, array, or conditional object of class names.

Components and props

ConnectWalletKitProvider

Sit this under the app’s ccc.Provider. It only stores shared defaults. It calls ccc.useCcc(), so it throws if CCC is missing. It never mounts ccc.Provider.

  • children (React.ReactNode) — The rest of the app.

  • defaults (ConnectWalletDefaults, default {}) — Shared look and formatting for every composition under the provider.

defaults

  • buttonClassName (ClassValue, default rounded-full bg-black text-white hover:opacity-90 dark:bg-white dark:text-black text-sm font-bold sm:text-base px-5 py-3) — Replaces the built-in colors, radius, and padding on ConnectWalletButton. Include dark: utilities if the button should keep that color in dark mode.

  • infoContainerClassName (ClassValue, same built-in appearance as the button) — Same role for the connected wallet pill (ConnectWalletInfoContainer).

  • imageClassName (ClassValue, default w-6 h-6) — Replaces the default size of the wallet icon.

  • balanceClassName (ClassValue, default font-semibold text-sm) — Replaces the default balance typography.

  • addressClassName (ClassValue, default text-xs font-normal) — Replaces the default address typography.

  • decimalPlaces (0–20 / DecimalPlaces, unset by default so up to 10 fraction digits show) — Shared balance precision. Digits are truncated, not rounded. 0 is a valid value.

  • withCurrency (boolean, default true) — When true, appends a CKB suffix after the balance.

  • frontChars (number, default 10) — Characters kept at the start of the truncated address.

  • endChars (number, default 6) — Characters kept at the end of the truncated address.

  • buttonLabel (React.ReactNode, default "Connect Wallet") — Label of ConnectWalletButton. A children prop on that button still wins.

  • didAvatarClassName (ClassValue, default w-6 h-6 rounded-full object-cover) — Replaces the default size and shape of ConnectWalletDidAvatar.

  • didNameClassName (ClassValue, default font-semibold text-sm) — Replaces the default typography of ConnectWalletDidName.

  • didIdClassName (ClassValue, default text-xs font-normal) — Replaces the default typography of ConnectWalletDidId.

  • didFrontChars (number, default 14) — Characters kept at the start of the truncated did:ckb: string.

  • didEndChars (number, default 6) — Characters kept at the end of the truncated did:ckb: string.

LayoutProvider

Same component as ConnectWalletKitProvider. Same props. Must sit under the app’s ccc.Provider.

  • children (React.ReactNode) — The rest of the app.

  • defaults (ConnectWalletDefaults, default {}) — Same as ConnectWalletKitProvider.

ConnectWallet

Local provider for one composition. It reads the CCC signer once and shares balance, address, loading, wallet, and open() with its children. Must sit under the app’s ccc.Provider.

  • children (React.ReactNode) — The button, the connected info, and any layout you put between them.

ConnectWalletButton

Renders only while no wallet is connected. Clicking it calls CCC open(). Hidden after connect.

  • className (ClassValue) — Merged after defaults.buttonClassName, so it overrides conflicting utilities on this button only.

  • children (React.ReactNode, default defaults.buttonLabel, then "Connect Wallet") — Replaces the button label.

ConnectWalletInfoContainer

Renders only after a wallet is connected. The whole pill calls open() again, which is how CCC shows account actions.

  • children (React.ReactNode) — Your layout for the icon, balance, and address.

  • className (ClassValue) — Merged after defaults.infoContainerClassName.

ConnectWalletInfoImage

The wallet icon from wallet.icon. Renders nothing until a wallet is connected.

  • className (ClassValue) — Merged after defaults.imageClassName. Built-in size is w-6 h-6.

ConnectWalletInfoBalance

Formats the signer balance with Intl.NumberFormat. When decimalPlaces is set (on the component or via defaults), extra digits are truncated, not rounded. Renders nothing until a wallet is connected.

  • decimalPlaces (0–20, default defaults.decimalPlaces, then up to 10 fraction digits) — Overrides the provider precision for this instance.

  • withCurrency (boolean, default defaults.withCurrency, then true) — When true, appends CKB after the number.

  • className (ClassValue) — Merged after defaults.balanceClassName.

ConnectWalletInfoAddress

Shows the recommended address. If the address is longer than frontChars + endChars, the middle is replaced with .... Renders nothing until a wallet is connected.

  • frontChars (number, default defaults.frontChars, then 10) — Characters kept at the start.

  • endChars (number, default defaults.endChars, then 6) — Characters kept at the end.

  • className (ClassValue) — Merged after defaults.addressClassName.

did:ckb

Optional. Place ConnectWalletDid inside ConnectWallet. It lists the live did:ckb cells owned by the connected lock and shares the newest one with its children. Nothing is fetched unless you render it, and it renders nothing before a wallet connects.

The display name and avatar come from services.profile in the DID document (displayName, avatar, bio), the convention used by did:ckb dashboards. A DID without a profile still has an identifier.

<ConnectWallet>
  <ConnectWalletButton />
  <ConnectWalletInfoContainer className="flex items-center gap-2">
    <ConnectWalletDid>
      <ConnectWalletDidAvatar fallback={<ConnectWalletInfoImage />} />
      <div className="flex flex-col items-start">
        <ConnectWalletDidName fallback={<ConnectWalletInfoAddress frontChars={6} endChars={4} />} />
        <ConnectWalletDidId />
      </div>
    </ConnectWalletDid>
  </ConnectWalletInfoContainer>
</ConnectWallet>

ConnectWalletDid

  • children (React.ReactNode) — The DID pieces, or anything that calls useConnectWalletDid().

  • resolve (DidResolver, default lists live did:ckb cells locked by the wallet) — Replace the lookup. Receives { client, signer, lock, address } and returns DidProfile[].

  • script (DidScript, default mainnet or testnet by client prefix) — Code hash and hash type of a custom did:ckb deployment. CCC’s KnownScript.DidCkb is used when the installed CCC has it.

  • pick ((dids: DidProfile[]) => DidProfile | undefined, default newest cell) — Choose which DID to show when the lock owns several.

useConnectWalletDid() returns { dids, did, isLoading, error, select } for a custom display. listDidsByLock, decodeDidCell, extractDidProfile, argsToDid, and DID_CKB_SCRIPTS are exported for use outside React.

ConnectWalletDidAvatar

The avatar from services.profile.avatar. Renders nothing while the lookup runs, and the fallback when the DID has no avatar.

  • className (ClassValue) — Merged after defaults.didAvatarClassName. Built-in is w-6 h-6 rounded-full object-cover.

  • fallback (React.ReactNode, default null) — Rendered when there is no avatar.

ConnectWalletDidName

The display name from services.profile.displayName. Renders the fallback when the DID has no name.

  • className (ClassValue) — Merged after defaults.didNameClassName. Built-in is font-semibold text-sm.

  • fallback (React.ReactNode, default null) — Rendered when there is no display name.

ConnectWalletDidId

The did:ckb: identifier, shortened with .... The full value is in the title attribute.

  • frontChars (number, default defaults.didFrontChars, then 14) — Characters kept at the start.

  • endChars (number, default defaults.didEndChars, then 6) — Characters kept at the end.

  • className (ClassValue) — Merged after defaults.didIdClassName.

  • fallback (React.ReactNode, default null) — Rendered when the lock owns no DID.

Prefer to copy the source

If you would rather vendor the files than depend on the package, copy these into the same folder in your app:

  • src/connect-wallet.tsx

  • src/utils.ts

  • src/connect-wallet-kit-provider.tsx

  • src/did-ckb.ts and src/connect-wallet-did.tsx (only if you want the DID pieces)

They have to stay together. Mount your own ccc.Provider around the kit provider. Then:

npm install @ckb-ccc/connector-react clsx tailwind-merge react react-dom

Tailwind already scans your project source on this path, so you do not add an @source rule.

Try it

The live demo at ckb-connect-wallet-kit.vercel.app has the same three usage examples, the did:ckb composition, and a components page that lists every prop.

I would like feedback from CKB app developers who are already on CCC, especially on:

  • Whether the CCC-first provider split matches how you already wrap apps

  • How the did:ckb pieces should behave when a lock owns several DIDs

  • Any missing pieces you still end up writing by hand

MIT licensed. Issues and PRs welcome on the repo.

Best,
Victor Okenwa

recent_posts.topic_title: Asset Price Oracle on Nervos Network
recent_posts.author: it44
recent_posts.content_text: Thanks for the very explicit design write-up, and for stating the limits plainly. One question on price_feed_type: the update rule is new.publish_time_ms > old.publish_time_ms. Is there also an upper bound on publish_time_ms relative to the transaction, for example against a header dep timestamp plus a small skew? If not, a single quorum-signed tick with a timestamp far in the future, from a publisher clock bug or a bad leader proposal that signers do not reject, would make every later honest update fail the strictly-newer check and freeze that feed cell until the committee is replaced and consumers re-pin. A consumer that compares publish_time_ms with a header timestamp could also read that future value as fresh. Do the signers refuse proposals outside their own clock window, and would an on-chain bound be acceptable?

topics.title: Routed Machine Payment Sessions on Fiber — Looking for Community Feedback

recent_posts.topic_title: Routed Machine Payment Sessions on Fiber — Looking for Community Feedback
recent_posts.author: it44
recent_posts.content_text: Thanks for asking before building. One design question on createPaymentSession({ budget }): where is the budget enforced? If it is a counter inside the SDK, the agent process (or a prompt-injected tool call) can bypass or reset it, so the cap is only as strong as that process. A harder bound is to make the budget the funded amount itself: one dedicated channel per session, funded with exactly `budget`, so the worst-case loss is the funding rather than the policy code. Related: with several providers paid in parallel, which component decides that two concurrent requests would together exceed the remaining budget, and if the counter cannot be read, does it deny or allow?
